Rajesh Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 6 October, 2025

Author: Milind Ramesh Phadke

Bench: Milind Ramesh Phadke

          NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993




                                                            1                           MCRC-23835-2022
                             IN     THE      HIGH COURT OF MADHYA PRADESH
                                                   AT GWALIOR
                                                       BEFORE
                                     HON'BLE SHRI JUSTICE MILIND RAMESH PHADKE
                                                ON THE 6 th OF OCTOBER, 2025
                                           MISC. CRIMINAL CASE No. 23835 of 2022
                                            RAJESH SHARMA AND OTHERS
                                                      Versus
                                     THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH AND OTHERS
                          Appearance:
                                  Shri Vijay Dutta Sharma - Advocate for petitioners.

                                  Shri Shishupal Singh Gurjar - Panel Lawyer for respondent No.1/State.
                                  Shri Nirmal Sharma - Advocate for respondent [R-2].

                                                                ORDER

This petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been filed by the petitioners seeking quashment of the FIR bearing Crime No. 124/2022, registered at Police Station Thatipur, District Gwalior, on 04.03.2022, for offences punishable under Sections 420, 406, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and all other consequential proceedings arising therefrom.

2. As per the prosecution case, the complainant, Avadhesh Sharma, son of Munni Ram Sharma, aged 37 years, resident of B-353, Suresh Nagar, Thatipur, Gwalior, proprietor of S.S. Construction, submitted a written complaint alleging that Gauri Construction Company, through its authorized partners Rajesh Kumar Sharma and Anupama Sharma, misappropriated and cheated him of a sum of Rs.12,14,000/-. It is alleged that in the year 2020, Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 2 MCRC-23835-2022 Gauri Construction Company was awarded a boring work contract by Gwalior Municipal Corporation. The complainant, who is closely related to the petitioners through his in-laws' side, was requested to provide financial assistance with assurance of repayment upon receipt of funds. Relying upon this assurance and family relations, the complainant transferred Rs.17,70,000/- by RTGS on 23.09.2020 and subsequently advanced Rs.13,75,000/- in cash between 09.10.2020 and 26.10.2021, making a total of Rs.31,45,000/-.

3. It is further alleged that the petitioners issued cheque No.000142 dated 05.01.2022 for Rs.19,31,000/- drawn on Bank of Baroda, Shivpuri Branch, and another cheque No.005946 dated 08.01.2022 for Rs.12,14,000/- drawn on Vijaya Bank, Shivpuri, towards repayment. The first cheque was dishonoured, and proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are pending. The second cheque was returned unpaid as Vijaya Bank had already ceased operations due to its merger with Bank of Baroda. The complainant alleges that the petitioners, having knowledge of the said merger, issued a cheque from a closed bank account with dishonest intention to defraud and misappropriate his funds.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that during the pendency of the present petition, the charge-sheet has been filed. It is urged that Gauri Construction is a duly constituted partnership firm comprising five partners; however, only two partners, namely Rajesh Kumar Sharma and Anupama Sharma, have been selectively implicated in the present criminal proceedings, leaving out the remaining partners without justification. It is Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 3 MCRC-23835-2022 contended that the transactions in question were purely commercial and financial in nature, arising out of business dealings between the parties. The cheque amounting to Rs.19,31,000/- was issued with the clear understanding that it would be presented only after the petitioners received payment from the Gwalior Municipal Corporation. Contrary to such understanding, the complainant prematurely presented the said cheque, which consequently got dishonoured. It is further submitted that another cheque amounting to Rs.12,14,000/- of Vijaya Bank was issued by the petitioners towards part payment; however, as Vijaya Bank had already merged with Bank of Baroda, the said cheque could not be honoured upon presentation. The complainant, despite being aware of such merger, deliberately presented the cheque only to initiate criminal prosecution against the petitioners. It is thus submitted that the dispute between the parties is essentially civil in nature, arising out of monetary transactions, but has been maliciously given a criminal colour to exert undue pressure upon the petitioners.

5. Per contra, learned counsel for respondent No.2 opposed the petition and submitted that the petitioners for the first time have accepted their liability in these proceedings, whereas in the proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, they have denied having issued any cheque. It is argued that the petitioners deliberately issued a cheque from a bank which had ceased to exist, thereby reflecting a fraudulent intention (mens rea) to cheat the complainant. From the surrounding circumstances, the presence of mens rea is clearly established, which is a necessary ingredient for constituting the offence under Section 420 IPC. It is further Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 4 MCRC-23835-2022 submitted that charges have already been framed against the petitioners, and the same have not been challenged.

6. Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record.

7. Before proceeding further, it would be appropriate to reproduce the relevant provisions of law.

8. Section 420, Indian Penal Code (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property):

"Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine."

9. Section 406, Indian Penal Code (Punishment for Criminal Breach of Trust):

"Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both."

10. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of International Advanced Research Centre For Powder Metallurgy and New Materials (ARCI) & Ors. v. Nimra Cerglass Technics Private Limited and Anr. reported in (2016) 1 SCC 348 while interpreting the definition of cheating has laid down the law as under :-

"15. The essential ingredients to attract Section 420 I.P.C. are: (i) cheating; (ii) dishonest inducement to deliver property or to make, Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 5 MCRC-23835-2022 alter or destroy any valuable security or anything which is sealed or signed or is capable of being converted into a valuable security and (iii) mens rea of the accused at the time of making the inducement. The making of a false representation is one of the essential ingredients to constitute the offence of cheating under Section 420 I.P.C. In order to bring a case for the offence of cheating, it is not merely sufficient to prove that a false representation had been made, but, it is further necessary to prove that the representation was false to the knowledge of the accused and was made in order to deceive the complainant.
16. Distinction between mere breach of contract and the cheating would depend upon the intention of the accused at the time of alleged inducement. If it is established that the intention of the accused was dishonest at the very time when he made a 1 Page 12 promise and entered into a transaction with the complainant to part with his property or money, then the liability is criminal and the accused is guilty of the offence of cheating. On the other hand, if all that is established that a representation made by the accused has subsequently not been kept, criminal liability cannot be foisted on the accused and the only right which the complainant acquires is the remedy for breach of contract in a civil court. Mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown at the beginning of the transaction. In S.W. Palanitkar & Ors. vs. State of Bihar & Anr. (2002) 1 SCC 241, this Court held as under:
"21 ......In order to constitute an offence of cheating, the intention to deceive should be in existence at the time when the inducement was made. It is necessary to show that a person had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise, to say that he committed an act of cheating. A mere failure to keep up promise subsequently cannot be presumed as an act leading to cheating."

The above view in Palanitkar's case was referred to and followed in Rashmi Jain vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. (2014) 13 SCC 553"

11. Furthermore, in the case of Delhi Race Club (1940) Ltd. and others v. State of U.P. and Another, reported in (2024) 10 SCC 690, it was laid down that-

"36. What can be discerned from the above is that the offences of criminal breach of trust (Section 406 IPC) and cheating (Section 420 IPC) have specific ingredients.
In order to constitute a criminal breach of trust (Section 406 IPC):
-
Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 6 MCRC-23835-2022
1) There must be entrustment with person for property or dominion over the property, and
2) The person entrusted: -
a) dishonestly misappropriated or converted property to his own use, or
b) dishonestly used or disposed of the property or willfully suffers any other person so to do in violation of:
i. any direction of law prescribing the method in which the trust is discharged; or ii. legal contract touching the discharge of trust (see: S.W.P. Palanitkar (supra).
Similarly, in respect of an offence under Section 420 IPC, the essential ingredients are: -
1) deception of any person, either by making a false or misleading representation or by other action or by omission;
2) fraudulently or dishonestly inducing any person to deliver any property, or
3) the consent that any persons shall retain any property and finally intentionally inducing that person to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit (see: Harmanpreet Singh Ahluwalia v. State of Punjab, (2009) 7 SCC 712 : (2009) 3 SCC (Cri) 620).

37. Further, in both the aforesaid sections, mens rea i.e. intention to defraud or the dishonest intention must be present, and in the case of cheating it must be there from the very beginning or inception.

38. In our view, the plain reading of the complaint fails to spell out any of the aforesaid ingredients noted above. We may only say, with a view to clear a serious misconception of law in the mind of the police as well as the courts below, that if it is a case of the complainant that offence of criminal breach of trust as defined under Section 405 of IPC, punishable under Section 406 of IPC, is committed by the accused, then in the same breath it cannot be said that the accused has also committed the offence of cheating as defined and explained in Section 415 of the IPC, punishable under Section 420 of the IPC.

39. Every act of breach of trust may not result in a penal offence of criminal breach of trust unless there is evidence of manipulating Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 7 MCRC-23835-2022 act of fraudulent misappropriation. An act of breach of trust involves a civil wrong in respect of which the person may seek his remedy for damages in civil courts but, any breach of trust with a mens rea, gives rise to a criminal prosecution as well. It has been held in Hari Prasad Chamaria v. Bishun Kumar Surekha & Ors., reported in (1973) 2 SCC 823 as under:

"4. We have heard Mr. Maheshwari on behalf of the appellant and are of the opinion that no case has been made out against the respondents under Section 420 Penal Code, 1860. For the purpose of the present appeal, we would assume that the various allegations of fact which have been made in the complaint by the appellant are correct. Even after making that allowance, we find that the complaint does not disclose the commission of any offence on the part of the respondents under Section 420 Penal Code, 1860. There is nothing in the complaint to show that the respondents had dishonest or fraudulent intention at the time the appellant parted with Rs. 35,000/- There is also nothing to indicate that the respondents induced the appellant to pay them Rs. 35,000/- by deceiving him. It is further not the case of the appellant that a representation was made, the respondents knew the same to be false. The fact that the respondents subsequently did not abide by their commitment that they would show the appellant to be the proprietor of Drang Transport Corporation and would also render accounts to him in the month of December might create civil liability on the respondents for the offence of cheating."

40. To put it in other words, the case of cheating and dishonest intention starts with the very inception of the transaction. But in the case of criminal breach of trust, a person who comes into possession of the movable property and receives it legally, but illegally retains it or converts it to his own use against the terms of the contract, then the question is, in a case like this, whether the retention is with dishonest intention or not, whether the retention involves criminal breach of trust or only a civil liability would depend upon the facts of each case.

41. The distinction between mere breach of contract and the offence of criminal breach of trust and cheating is a fine one. In case of cheating, the intention of the accused at the time of inducement should be looked into which may be judged by a subsequent conduct, but for this, the subsequent conduct is not the sole test. Mere breach of contract cannot give rise to a criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right from the beginning of the transaction i.e. the time when the offence is said to have been committed. Therefore, it is this intention, which is the gist of the offence."

12. A careful perusal of the FIR and the material collected during Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 8 MCRC-23835-2022 investigation reveals that at no point of time, the liability was/is disputed by the petitioners, except for non-issuance of cheque and misusing of the cheque of a bank merged. Inception of deceit is to be reckoned from the date when money was advanced, but the contents of the FIR do not disclose such intention of the petitioners at that moment, and the dispute essentially arises out of a commercial transaction between the parties. The allegations do not disclose the existence of any fraudulent or dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, which is a sine qua non for constituting an offence under Section 420 IPC. Similarly, the ingredients of Section 406 IPC are also not satisfied, as there is no material to indicate that the petitioners were entrusted with property or dominion over funds in a fiduciary capacity, or that they misappropriated the same in breach of such trust. The transactions appear to have been carried out in the course of business dealings between two firms, and the alleged failure to repay or honour cheques would, at best, give rise to civil liability and proceedings under the Negotiable Instruments Act.

13. On perusal of the FIR and the material collected during investigation, it is evident that the complainant and petitioners were closely related and were engaged in a series of business transactions. The money was advanced to assist in execution of a municipal contract, and cheques were issued in acknowledgement of such liability. The allegations, even if accepted in their entirety, do not reveal the existence of dishonest intention or entrustment from the inception of the transaction. The dispute thus falls squarely within the domain of a civil liability for recovery or for adjudication Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:24993 9 MCRC-23835-2022 under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

14. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Satish Mehra v. State (N.C.T. of Delhi) and Another , AIR 2013 SC 506 , has held that the inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. are wide and plenary in nature and may be exercised at any stage of criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice. It has been observed that where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint do not prima facie disclose the commission of a cognizable offence, the accused should not be compelled to undergo the rigours of a protracted criminal trial.

15. In the present case, even if the entire allegations in the FIR are taken at their face value, they merely disclose a civil dispute arising out of monetary transactions. The initiation of criminal proceedings appears to be a device to settle personal and financial scores. Continuance of such prosecution would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.

16. Accordingly, this Court is of the considered view that the FIR bearing Crime No.124/2022 registered at Police Station Thatipur, District Gwalior, for offences punishable under Sections 420, 406, and 34 IPC against the petitioners and all consequential proceedings arising therefrom, deserve to be and are hereby quashed.

17. The petition is accordingly allowed. No order as to costs.

(MILIND RAMESH PHADKE) JUDGE ojha Signature Not Verified Signed by: YOGENDRA OJHA Signing time: 10/9/2025 10:23:37 AM
